claims.text: The baseline material is a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without engineered second-phase precipitates.
The baseline CoCrFeNi alloy exhibits increasing friction and wear, especially at elevated temperatures approaching 800 °C.
A controlled nanoscale self-lubricating precipitate can be incorporated into the CoCrFeNi matrix through alloying or processing.
The introduced precipitates will be uniformly dispersed within the CoCrFeNi matrix.
Heat and mechanical stress during sliding will activate the precipitates as local sites for lubricious surface-layer formation.
The precipitates will preferentially oxidize or transform during sliding.
Oxidation or phase transformation of the precipitates will produce a continuous, stable lubricious tribofilm on the contact surface.
The tribofilm will reduce direct metal-to-metal contact.
Reduced direct metal-to-metal contact will lower friction and wear.
The modified alloy will have lower coefficients of friction than the baseline alloy throughout the range from room temperature to 800 °C.
The modified alloy will have lower wear rates than the baseline alloy throughout the range from room temperature to 800 °C.
Near 700 °C, the modified alloy may attain friction levels observed in comparable self-lubricating systems.
The intervention is expected to be effective under controlled moderate loads in ambient oxidizing air.
The intervention may not remain effective under extreme loads, inert atmospheres, or substantially different environments.
The precipitate composition, size, distribution, and oxidation kinetics required for optimal tribofilm formation are not yet determined.
The activation temperature and cyclic durability of the lubricious film require verification.
